title: Five Fruits a Day May Not Save Your Heart. A 30,000-Person Study Says It Is the Type That Matters.
excerpt: Fewer than one in four adults hit the flavanol threshold linked to cardiovascular protection — but traditional South Asian staples like green tea, fava beans and berries could close the gap overnight.
body:
The global consensus has been simple for decades: eat five servings of fruits and vegetables a day and your heart will thank you. A sprawling new study across two continents now says that advice, while sound, is dangerously incomplete.

Researchers from the University of Reading, Harvard Medical School, the University of California at Davis and Mars, Inc. analysed dietary biomarker data from more than 30,000 adults in the United States and the United Kingdom. Their conclusion, published in the journal *Food & Function*, is blunt: following standard dietary guidelines for fruit and vegetable intake does not deliver enough flavanols — a class of plant compounds with proven cardiovascular benefits — to meaningfully protect the heart.

Fewer than 25 per cent of participants who dutifully ate their five-a-day reached an estimated flavanol intake of 500 milligrams per day, the threshold linked to measurable cardiovascular benefits in the landmark COSMOS trial. Among participants in the EPIC-Norfolk cohort in Britain, the numbers were even worse: fewer than one in five cleared the bar.

"Most people assume that eating plenty of fruit and vegetables covers this, but what this research shows is that the specific choices you make matter far more than the total amount," said lead author Javier Ottaviani of the University of Reading. "Flavanols can significantly reduce the risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, but only if you consume enough of them."

## The Flavanol Gap

Flavanols are a subclass of flavonoids found in varying concentrations across the plant kingdom. They work by keeping blood vessels flexible, reducing arterial stiffness and lowering blood pressure. The COSMOS trial, which followed more than 21,000 adults aged 60 and above, established the 500 mg daily threshold as the point at which cardiovascular death risk drops appreciably.

The problem is that not all fruits and vegetables are created equal when it comes to flavanols. A banana has almost none. A portion of iceberg lettuce is negligible. Even carrots, the poster child of healthy eating, contribute very little.



> **"Green tea is a daily fixture in millions of households."**


The richest sources are far more specific: green tea delivers roughly 200 mg per cup. A handful of blackberries provides 125 mg. A medium apple with its skin offers 110 mg. Broad beans, also known as fava beans, deliver 140 mg per small portion. Two cups of green tea and a handful of berries would get most adults past the line.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora


![Your Heart — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/5/52/Joyner_Lucas_%26_J._Cole_-_Your_Heart.jpg)


For South Asians, the findings carry a particular sting — and a surprising silver lining.

The sting: South Asians already face a disproportionately high burden of cardiovascular disease. The MASALA study and multiple cohort analyses have shown that heart attacks strike South Asians roughly a decade earlier than other populations, even after adjusting for conventional risk factors like cholesterol, blood pressure and diabetes.

The silver lining: many traditional South Asian dietary staples are naturally rich in the exact compounds the study identifies as protective. Green tea is a daily fixture in millions of households. Rajma (kidney beans) and chana (chickpeas) contribute meaningful flavanol doses. Seasonal fruits like jamun (Indian blackberry), amla (Indian gooseberry) and pomegranate are flavanol-dense. Even the humble guava, widely consumed across the subcontinent, outperforms most Western fruits on flavanol content.

The research suggests that diaspora families who have drifted toward Western dietary patterns — replacing green tea with coffee, swapping dal and sabzi for sandwiches and pasta — may be inadvertently widening their flavanol gap at precisely the age when cardiovascular risk accelerates.

## What the Science Says to Do

Professor Gunter Kuhnle of the University of Reading offered a practical prescription: "Including blueberries, plums, blackberries, broad beans or cherries — washed down with green tea — in your five-a-day may be the best way to a healthier heart."

A rough daily target of 500 mg can be hit with two-and-a-half cups of green tea alone, or a combination of one apple, a portion of berries and a cup of black tea. The key is intentionality: swapping a low-flavanol fruit for a high-flavanol one within the same calorie envelope.

The study examined estimated flavanol consumption through validated urinary biomarkers, not self-reported intake, lending it unusual rigour. But it did not directly measure cardiovascular outcomes, meaning the 500 mg threshold is drawn from prior interventional data rather than proven anew.

## What Comes Next

The researchers argue that governments should consider establishing specific dietary reference values for flavanols, rather than relying on blanket fruit-and-vegetable targets that may leave populations nutritionally exposed.

For diaspora families, the takeaway is more immediate. The heart-protective compounds that Western dietitians are only now quantifying have been present in traditional South Asian food systems for centuries. The challenge is not discovering them — it is remembering to keep eating them.
